title: Shishupala
hook: Shishupala challenges Krishna to fight, and Krishna finally speaks: the pardons are used up
carry: name your limit, kindly and clearly

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma told of Shishupala's birth, and Krishna's promise to his aunt: a hundred pardons. His silence is a promise kept.

Bhishma's story should have cooled the room. It does the opposite. Shishupala hears that he's been spared all his life by Krishna's promise, and he isn't grateful. He's insulted. He turns from Bhishma to Krishna himself and calls him out: stand up and fight me. For the first time in this whole scene, the challenge is aimed straight at the silent guest, with every king watching. And after all that waiting, Krishna speaks.
screen: `THE STORY DOESN'T COOL HIM.` → `FIGHT ME.` → `THE SILENT GUEST STANDS.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't answer Shishupala first. He turns to the kings. In the telling, he lays out what Shishupala has done: wrongs against Krishna's own people, some of them while Krishna was far away and couldn't defend them. He reminds the hall that Shishupala is his aunt's son, and that for her sake he has borne all of it. Then comes the line the whole week has waited for, in effect: the hundred are full. The promise has been kept to the end. Shishupala doesn't back down. He laughs at Krishna and dares him to do his worst. So Krishna calls to mind his discus, the spinning weapon that is his in the stories, and it comes to his hand. In front of all the kings, he strikes, and the king of Chedi falls. The order matters. Krishna doesn't strike at the first insult, or the tenth, or when Bhima wants to. He waits until his word to his aunt has been fully kept, and even then he explains himself to the room first. Patience and judgment are two parts of the same thing here. Patience has a shape and a limit, and the limit was set long ago, in love, for a frightened mother. Some readers find the ending hard. Some find it just. The poem gives us the waiting, the warning and the blow, and lets us hold all three.
screen: `KRISHNA SPEAKS TO THE KINGS.` · `FOR HIS AUNT'S SAKE, HE BORE IT.` · `THE HUNDRED ARE FULL.` · `THE DISCUS COMES TO HIS HAND.` · then, large: `PATIENCE WITH A SHAPE AND A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind somewhere you've been patient for a long time, with a person or with a habit of your own, and ask quietly: where is the limit here? You don't have to decide anything now; breathe in steadiness, and breathe out the strain of waiting. If you pray, you can ask for clarity about it; if not, rest with the question.
Shishupala. The king who challenged Krishna once too often, after a hundred pardons kept for his mother's sake had run out.
Your line: name your limit, kindly and clearly. Krishna's was set long before the hall. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Hindu retellings and devotional art, the Sudarshana discus is one of Krishna's signs, and some tellers present the end of Shishupala as the moment his long patience reaches its promised limit.

fork.setup: you're Krishna. Shishupala has used up every pardon you promised his mother, and now he dares you to fight. what do you do first?
fork.reveal: Krishna first tells the kings what Shishupala has done and why he bore it, and only then calls his discus.

original.note: Sanskrit cakra: wheel or discus; Krishna's discus comes to his hand at the end of the scene.

trapdoor: what you thought: Krishna finally lost his temper.
what it means: he waited until his promise of a hundred pardons was fully kept, then explained himself and acted.
what a scholar hears: the scene joins patience and judgment, with the limit fixed long before by a promise to a mother.

chat.says: If Krishna was so patient, why did he finally strike Shishupala?
options: His promise of a hundred pardons was fully kept, and he explained himself first.
He lost his temper at the very first insult and couldn't hold back.
Bhima begged him to, so Krishna struck to spare Bhima the fight.
chat.meaning: Krishna waited until the hundred pardons promised to his aunt were full, told the kings why, and only then acted.

discus.meaning: Krishna's spinning weapon in the stories, called Sudarshana

Bhima.meaning: second Pandava brother, famed for strength and anger

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sisupala-badha Parva (Shishupala challenges Krishna; Krishna addresses the kings, recounts his offenses and his promise; the discus)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Krishna addresses the kings and lists Shishupala's past wrongs against the Yadavas, some committed while Krishna was away; the specific wrongs are deliberately not named.
Confirm Krishna says, in sense, that the pardons promised to his aunt are now exhausted, and that Shishupala laughs and taunts him.
Confirm the discus comes to Krishna's hand when he thinks of it.
The death is described briefly and without gore on purpose.
